I usually quote the character and the work the character is from.
Character, as it can always be looked up who the author was. Without the character you miss other context that may be necessary.

The Character.

The author wrote it, but through the frame of a character, so I credit the character.

If the author had simply written an essay, then I would credit the author.

People that use pithy quotes from books might simply add the authors name at the end, but this is for ease of recognition for those that might not have read the book. Regardless of how anyone might feel, the character in the book is saying the lines, it's coming from them, not the author directly.

Qagyuhl wedding party pulls ashore in two canoes. The bride and groom are standing in the stern. By Edward Curtis. British Columbia. c. 1914

Edward Curtis (February 16, 1868 – October 19, 1952) was an American ethnologist and photographer of the American West and of Native American peoples.

At the end of 1912, Curtis decided to create a feature film depicting Native American life, partly as a way of improving his financial situation and partly because film technology had improved to the point where it was conceivable to create and screen films more than a few minutes long. Curtis chose the Kwakiutl tribe of the Queen Charlotte Strait region of the Central Coast of British Columbia, Canada, for his subject. This film, entitled In the Land of the Head Hunters, was the first feature-length film whose cast was composed entirely of Native North Americans, the first feature film made in British Columbia, and is the oldest surviving feature film made in Canada.
